e.meaning: he lives; the Arabic name of John the Baptist
e.etymology: The Qur'anic name of John the Baptist. In Arabic it reads as he lives, from the root for life, while the figure corresponds to the Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
namesakes: Yahya Abdul-Mateen II (actor in Aquaman and Watchmen)

e.etymology: A pet form of Jim, the short form of James, which is the English form of the Hebrew Jacob. Long given as a name in its own right.
namesakes: Jimmy Stewart (film star of It's a Wonderful Life)

assoc.t: to jimmy: pry open a door, window or lock
Jimmy Choo, luxury shoe brand
Jimmy John's sandwich chain
Jimmy Dean breakfast sausage and sandwiches

e.etymology: The Italian form of Roland, from Germanic words for fame and land. Roland was Charlemagne's legendary knight, hero of the Italian epic Orlando Furioso; Shakespeare used Orlando in As You Like It.
namesakes: Orlando Bloom (actor in The Lord of the Rings and Pirates of the Caribbean)

assoc.t: Orlando, Florida, home of Walt Disney World

e.etymology: A short form of Alexander that arose in Scotland. Alexander comes from Greek alexein, to defend, and aner, man.
namesakes: Alec Guinness (actor who played Obi-Wan Kenobi)

assoc.t: smart alec: a know-it-all

e.etymology: A spelling of Annika, the Swedish pet form of Anna, from Hebrew Hannah, grace. The same spelling is also used by Indian families.
namesakes: Anika Noni Rose (actress, voice of Tiana in The Princess and the Frog)

e.etymology: A respelling of Weston, an English place name and surname from Old English west and tun, the western settlement.

assoc.t: Westin, Marriott's upscale hotel chain (same sound)

e.etymology: The Spanish and Catalan form of Raymond, from Frankish Raginmund: ragin, counsel, and mund, protection.
A Yorkshire occupational surname for a peddler or carter who carried packs. Its use as a first name follows Mick Jagger of the Rolling Stones.
namesakes: Mick Jagger (lead singer of the Rolling Stones)

assoc.t: Mick Jagger, Rolling Stones frontman
Moves Like Jagger, 2011 Maroon 5 hit song

e.etymology: The feminine form of Alexius and Alexis, from Greek alexein, to defend or help.

assoc.t: alexia, the medical term for losing the ability to read
Alexia frozen fries and onion rings

e.etymology: From Arabic abd, servant, and Allah, God. It was the name of the Prophet Muhammad's father and is one of the most common names in the Muslim world.
A respelling of Ezra, from Hebrew ezra, help. Ezra was the priest and scribe who led exiles back to Jerusalem in the Old Testament book named for him.
From Old French Tifinie, from Greek Theophania, appearance of God, the feast of Epiphany. A medieval name for girls born at Epiphany, it returned after the 1961 film Breakfast at Tiffany's.
namesakes: Tiffany (1980s pop singer of I Think We're Alone Now)

assoc.t: Tiffany & Co., luxury jeweler with the robin's-egg blue box
Tiffany lamp, stained-glass lamp style

e.etymology: From the US state, whose name comes through Spanish montaña from Latin montana, mountainous. It became a place-name choice for girls and boys in the 1990s.

assoc.t: Montana, US state in the northern Rockies
Hannah Montana, Disney pop star played by Miley Cyrus
Joe Montana, Hall of Fame 49ers quarterback
Tony Montana, Al Pacino's gangster in Scarface

e.etymology: The English word ever, always, used as a modern word name. Ever is also an established male name in Latin America, and the Hebrew form of the biblical Eber.
A respelling of Cadence, the English word for a rhythmic flow or the close of a musical phrase, from Latin cadere, to fall.
A spelling of Liliana, an elaboration of Lillian. Lillian probably began as a pet form of Elizabeth and was soon tied to the lily, Latin lilium.
A pet form of names beginning Jer- or Ger-, chiefly Gerald, Jerome, Jeremy and Jeremiah. Americans have given it as a full name since the 19th century.
namesakes: Jerry Rice (Hall of Fame wide receiver)

assoc.t: Jerry, the mouse in the Tom and Jerry cartoons
Ben & Jerry's ice cream
Jerry, old British wartime slang for a German

e.etymology: A variant of Rosaline and Rosalind. Rosalind is Germanic, from hros, horse, and lind, gentle, but has long been read as Spanish rosa linda, pretty rose. Many parents now see Rose plus -lyn.
A 19th-century coinage that joins Lou, the short form of Louise, to the ending -ella. It was widely used in the US around 1900 and has returned with other names of that era.
A spelling of Ashlyn, which blends Ashley with Lynn and is also treated as an English form of the Irish Aisling, dream or vision.
A respelling of Harley, an English place name and surname from Old English hara, hare, and leah, clearing or meadow.

assoc.t: Harley-Davidson motorcycles, called Harleys (same sound)
Harley Quinn, DC Comics antihero (same sound)

e.etymology: A modern name built from Ali- and Anna, close in sound to Eliana, Aliana and Ariana. It has no settled meaning of its own.
The French word for sun, from Latin sol. As a given name it is used mainly in the United States.
namesakes: Soleil Moon Frye (actress who played Punky Brewster)

assoc.t: Cirque du Soleil, the acrobatic circus company

e.etymology: A modern coinage that adds the -lynn ending to Ember, the English word for a glowing coal.
From the title of Mary Magdalene in the New Testament: Greek Magdalene, woman from Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee whose Aramaic name means tower. The same source gives Madeline.

assoc.t: Magdalena River, the main river of Colombia

e.etymology: A modern American name that pairs the Ka- opening with the -iyah ending of Aaliyah and Amiyah. It has no settled meaning.
A spelling of Cody, an Irish surname anglicized from Ó Cuidighthigh, descendant of the helpful one. The name spread in the US through the fame of Buffalo Bill Cody.
namesakes: Kodi Smit-McPhee (actor in The Power of the Dog)

assoc.t: Kodi, free open-source media player software

e.etymology: A recent American coinage that puts an R in front of Wyatt, in the style of Ryan, Ryder and Ryker.
e.note: Sounds the same as the word riot.

e.etymology: A phonetic English spelling of Caitlin, the Irish form of Catherine, which came through Old French Cateline. Catherine's Greek source is obscure but was long linked with katharos, pure.
From Sanskrit rohana, ascending, a common name in India. Separately, Rohan is an Irish surname related to Rowan and Ruane, and the name of a noble family from Rohan in Brittany.

assoc.t: Rohan, realm of the horse lords in The Lord of the Rings

e.etymology: An English place name and surname from Old English byxe, box tree, and leah, clearing. Bexley is a borough of London and a suburb of Columbus, Ohio.

assoc.t: Bexley, borough of southeast London

e.etymology: A respelling of Bailey, an English surname for a bailiff or steward, from Old French bailli. The -lee ending follows Kaylee and Haylee.

assoc.t: Baileys Irish Cream liqueur (same sound)
